title: Cosmology II: Friedmann dynamics and model universes
scope: How Einstein's equations drive the scale factor of a homogeneous, isotropic universe: Newtonian cosmology as a warm-up and its boundary problem; the FRW model with a perfect-fluid source; the Friedmann, second Friedmann and acceleration equations; the fluid equation and the dilution of matter, radiation and vacuum energy; vacuum energy as a p = -rho fluid, negative pressure and the condition for acceleration; critical density, density parameters, the cosmic sum rule and the dimensionless Friedmann equation; qualitative analysis through the effective potential, the classification of Friedmann models and the Omega_m-Omega_Lambda plane; the catalogue of model universes (Milne, Einstein-de Sitter, radiation-dominated, de Sitter, matter-plus-Lambda, closed and open dust, negative Lambda, Einstein static and its instability, Lemaitre, Eddington-Lemaitre, bouncing); de Sitter and anti-de Sitter as maximally symmetric spacetimes; the explicit big bang and big crunch of Friedmann models, the Hubble time and age of the universe, Hubble friction for a scalar field, anisotropic Bianchi and Kasner models, and the steady-state alternative. Robertson-Walker geometry, redshift, distances and horizons belong to cosmological-kinematics; observations, Lambda-CDM parameters, thermal history and inflation to physical-cosmology.

concepts.title: Newtonian cosmology
aliases: Newtonian derivation of the Friedmann equation
concepts.summary: A uniform, expanding ball of self-gravitating dust treated with Newtonian gravity: energy conservation for a test mass on a comoving shell gives an equation for the scale factor with exactly the form of the Friedmann equation, with the curvature term reinterpreted as the shell's total energy.

names: Newtonian derivation of the Friedmann equation

merged_from: Newtonian derivation of the Friedmann equation
concepts.notes: Taught as a heuristic preview in all three books (GA Example 17.1, DIV ch24 point galaxies with an optional force proportional to distance for Lambda, SCH ch13 expanding cloud with accumulated Doppler shifts). Stress that the matching of form hides a different interpretation of the terms.

concepts.title: Boundary problem of Newtonian cosmology
concepts.summary: For an infinite uniform medium Poisson's equation has no unique solution: the Newtonian field inside depends on the shape of a distant boundary, so an edgeless Newtonian cosmology is not well defined, whereas in general relativity dynamics are fixed by what lies inside past light cones.
concepts.notes: SCH ch13 uses it to explain why cosmology became a physical science only with general relativity (Exercise 13.3).

concepts.title: Friedmann-Robertson-Walker model
concepts.summary: The standard relativistic cosmological model: a Robertson-Walker metric, justified by the cosmological principle and Weyl's postulate, whose scale factor is determined by Einstein's equations (with cosmological constant) sourced by a homogeneous perfect fluid. Solving for different curvature, Lambda and matter content gives the family of Friedmann models.
concepts.notes: DIV ch24 lists the three ingredients (cosmological principle, Weyl postulate, GR with Lambda). The purely geometric k = +1, 0, -1 slices belong to cosmological-kinematics.

concepts.title: Perfect-fluid model of the cosmic contents
aliases: perfect-fluid model of the cosmic contents
concepts.summary: Galaxies and radiation are smoothed into a homogeneous perfect fluid at rest in comoving coordinates, with density and pressure depending only on cosmic time; any bulk flow or anisotropic stress would pick out a direction and break isotropy.

names: perfect-fluid model of the cosmic contents

merged_from: perfect-fluid model of the cosmic contents
concepts.notes: With no internal interactions the cosmic fluid is dust (GA ch15); radiation is the p = rho/3 case.

concepts.title: Friedmann equation
aliases: energy equation for the scale factor
concepts.summary: The time-time Einstein equation for a Robertson-Walker universe: H^2 = (adot/a)^2 = 8 pi G rho/3 + Lambda/3 - k/a^2. It fixes the expansion rate from the total energy density and spatial curvature, and, having no second derivative, acts as a constraint on the initial data rather than an evolution equation.
merged_from: Ricci tensor of the Robertson-Walker metric
concepts.notes: Books derive it by substituting the Robertson-Walker Einstein (or Ricci) tensor in a comoving orthonormal frame; the adot-dot terms cancel in G_tt. SCH notes only G_tt needs computing since the Bianchi identity links it to G_rr. The curvature tensor of the RW metric itself belongs to cosmological-kinematics. "Friedmann equations" (plural) names the pair; see second-friedmann-equation and acceleration-equation.

concepts.title: Second Friedmann equation
concepts.summary: The space-space Einstein equation for a Robertson-Walker universe, 2 addot/a + (adot/a)^2 + k/a^2 = -8 pi G p + Lambda, which contains the acceleration of the scale factor and is sourced by pressure. For an expanding universe it is not independent: it follows from differentiating the first Friedmann equation and using the fluid equation.
concepts.notes: GA Example 17.4 shows the redundancy: one Friedmann equation plus energy conservation plus an equation of state closes the system (when adot is nonzero).

concepts.title: Fluid equation
aliases: first law for the expanding universe
concepts.summary: Energy conservation for the cosmic fluid, rhodot + 3(adot/a)(rho + p) = 0, equivalently d(rho a^3) = -p d(a^3): the energy in a comoving volume falls both by dilution and by the p dV work done as the volume grows. It is the time component of the covariant conservation of the stress-energy tensor in an FRW spacetime.

names: adiabatic expansion of the cosmic fluid

merged_from: adiabatic expansion of the cosmic fluid
concepts.notes: GA derives it thermodynamically from adiabatic (dS = 0) expansion of a comoving volume; SCH via Christoffel symbols (Exercise 13.14); DIV by combining the two Friedmann equations and identifying the result with the contracted Bianchi identity.

concepts.title: Acceleration equation
concepts.summary: Combining the two Friedmann equations eliminates the curvature and velocity terms: addot/a = -(4 pi G/3)(rho + 3p) + Lambda/3. Ordinary matter and positive pressure decelerate the expansion, with pressure counting three times, while positive Lambda accelerates it.

concepts.title: Scaling of energy density with the scale factor
aliases: rho proportional to a^-3 and a^-4
scaling of densities with the scale factor
concepts.summary: Integrating the fluid equation for a fixed equation of state gives how each component dilutes: pressureless matter rho proportional to a^-3 (fixed particle number in a growing volume), radiation a^-4 (dilution plus redshift of each quantum), and vacuum energy constant. Hence radiation dominates early, matter later and Lambda last.

names: scaling of energy density with the scale factor
scaling of energy density with the scale factor
scaling of density with scale factor
scaling of densities with the scale factor

merged_from: scaling of energy density with the scale factor
scaling of density with scale factor
scaling of densities with the scale factor
concepts.notes: General rule: for p = w rho, rho scales as a^(-3(1+w)). GA Exercise 17.3 treats the boundary case rho proportional to a^-2 (p = -rho/3), which gives coasting expansion a proportional to t.

concepts.title: Vacuum energy as a perfect fluid
aliases: vacuum energy as a cosmological constant
vacuum energy as an effective cosmological constant
concepts.summary: Moving the Lambda g term to the source side turns the cosmological constant into a perfect fluid of constant energy density rho_Lambda = Lambda/(8 pi G) and pressure p = -rho_Lambda. Conversely, any vacuum energy must have a Lorentz-invariant stress-energy tensor proportional to the metric, so it behaves exactly like a cosmological constant and does not dilute as space expands.

names: vacuum energy as a cosmological constant
vacuum energy as an effective cosmological constant
vacuum energy as a perfect fluid

merged_from: vacuum energy as a cosmological constant
vacuum energy as a perfect fluid
vacuum energy as an effective cosmological constant
concepts.notes: GA ch41 applies it to a scalar field frozen at potential value U, which acts as Lambda = 8 pi U and drives inflation. Why the observed value is so small (the cosmological constant problem) belongs to quantum-gravity-and-beyond; dark energy as an observed component belongs to physical-cosmology.

concepts.title: Negative pressure and cosmic repulsion
aliases: repulsive gravity of a cosmological constant
concepts.summary: A component whose pressure is negative (a tension) contributes rho + 3p to the gravitating density; for vacuum energy with p = -rho this is -2 rho, so its gravity is repulsive and it accelerates the expansion even though its energy density is positive.
concepts.notes: GA ch45 Exercise 45.5 shows the linearized potential of vacuum energy grows as -Lambda r^2/6, pushing test bodies apart. A negative Lambda acts attractively, like ordinary matter.

concepts.title: Condition for accelerated expansion
aliases: violation of the strong energy condition
concepts.summary: From the acceleration equation, the expansion speeds up (addot > 0) only if the dominant content satisfies rho + 3p < 0, i.e. p < -rho/3, which violates the strong energy condition; for a homogeneous scalar field this means its kinetic energy is less than its potential energy.
concepts.notes: GA ch41 uses the scalar-field form as the criterion for when inflation ends. The observed acceleration belongs to physical-cosmology.

concepts.title: Critical density
concepts.summary: The total energy density rho_c = 3H^2/(8 pi G) that makes a Friedmann universe spatially flat at the current expansion rate; today it is of order 10^-26 kg m^-3, a few hydrogen atoms per cubic metre.
concepts.notes: SCH presents it by treating the expansion as a "Hubble energy density" that must balance curvature, matter and Lambda terms. DIV uses the name for the present value and later reintroduces a time-dependent rho_crit(t).

concepts.title: Density parameter
concepts.summary: The ratio Omega = rho/rho_c of an energy density to the critical density, defined for each component (Omega_m for matter, Omega_r for radiation, Omega_Lambda = Lambda/3H_0^2 for vacuum energy) and for their total; the present values together with H_0 specify an FRW model and are the targets of observation.
concepts.notes: Each Omega generally changes with time; a superscript or subscript 0 marks present values. Measured values (Omega_Lambda about 0.7, Omega_m about 0.3) belong to physical-cosmology.

concepts.title: Curvature density parameter
concepts.summary: The curvature term of the Friedmann equation written as if it were a density fraction, Omega_k = -k/(a_0^2 H_0^2) (equivalently a curvature energy density -3k/(8 pi G a^2)); it is positive for open, zero for flat and negative for closed universes.
concepts.notes: The sign convention makes Omega_k positive for k = -1; DIV notes it equals twice the "energy" of the particle analogy.

concepts.title: Cosmic sum rule
concepts.summary: Evaluated today and divided by H_0^2, the Friedmann equation states that the density parameters of all components plus the curvature parameter add to exactly one, Omega_r + Omega_m + Omega_Lambda + Omega_k = 1, so the spatial curvature follows from the measured contents.

concepts.title: Density parameter and spatial geometry
concepts.summary: Rewriting the Friedmann equation as k/adot^2 = Omega - 1 shows that total density relative to critical fixes the sign of the curvature: Omega > 1 gives a closed (spherical) universe, Omega = 1 flat and Omega < 1 open (hyperbolic); since k is constant, the sign of Omega - 1 can never change.
concepts.notes: With Lambda = 0 this also tied geometry to fate (closed recollapses, open expands forever); a nonzero Lambda breaks that link.

concepts.title: Multi-component Friedmann equation
aliases: Friedmann equations for a multi-component universe
Friedmann equation with radiation, matter and Lambda
concepts.summary: The Friedmann equation with the total density split into components that each scale with their own power of the scale factor: H^2 = (8 pi G/3)[rho_r0 (a_0/a)^4 + rho_m0 (a_0/a)^3 + rho_Lambda] - k/a^2, so knowing the densities and expansion rate at one time determines a(t) for all times.

names: Friedmann equations for a multi-component universe

merged_from: Friedmann equations for a multi-component universe

concepts.title: Dimensionless Friedmann equation
aliases: E(z) form of the Friedmann equation
concepts.summary: Measuring the scale factor against its present value and time in Hubble times turns the Friedmann equation into (dx/dt~)^2 = Omega_r/x^2 + Omega_m/x + Omega_Lambda x^2 + Omega_k, so the density parameters alone fix the shape of the expansion history while H_0 only sets the time scale.

names: dimensionless Friedmann equation in density parameters

merged_from: dimensionless Friedmann equation in density parameters
concepts.notes: DIV ch26 highlights that Omega_r, Omega_m, Omega_Lambda and H_0 completely specify a radiation-matter-Lambda FRW model (with R_0 = 1/(H_0 |Omega_k|^1/2) when k is nonzero). Equivalent H(z) = H_0 E(z) form with x = 1/(1+z).

concepts.title: Effective potential for the scale factor
aliases: qualitative analysis of the Friedmann equation
concepts.summary: Writing the Friedmann equation as (1/2) adot^2 + V(a) = E turns cosmic expansion into one-dimensional motion of a particle in a potential: the universe can only be where V is below E, points where V = E are turning points, and the dominant term at small or large a gives power-law or exponential behaviour.

names: effective potential for the scale factor
effective potential for the scale factor
qualitative analysis of the Friedmann equation
effective potential for the scale factor

merged_from: effective potential for the scale factor
qualitative analysis of the Friedmann equation
concepts.notes: SCH compares it to the Schwarzschild orbit method; DIV ch25 uses the equivalent Rdot^2 = F(R) form to sketch every dust model, and ch26 the dimensionless potential V = -(1/2)(Omega_m/x + Omega_r/x^2 + Omega_Lambda x^2) with E = Omega_k/2.

concepts.title: Classification of Friedmann models
concepts.summary: Dust Friedmann models fall into a finite set of qualitatively distinct histories labelled by the curvature index k and by the sign of Lambda and its size relative to the critical value: big-bang models that expand forever, recollapse, or loiter, and models that bounce or approach a static state.
concepts.notes: DIV ch25 Fig. 25.1 gives 14 hand-drawn cases (I: k = -1, II: k = 0, III: k = +1); GA ch18 presents the same catalogue as numbered Universes 0-11 in a summary grid.

concepts.title: Omega_m-Omega_Lambda plane
concepts.summary: With radiation neglected, each point (Omega_m, Omega_Lambda) is an FRW model, and curves divide the plane: Omega_m + Omega_Lambda = 1 separates closed from open, Omega_Lambda = Omega_m/2 separates accelerating from decelerating, and curves from the effective potential separate recollapse from eternal expansion and big-bang models from bouncing ones.
concepts.notes: The no-big-bang and recollapse boundaries come from setting the maximum of the potential equal to E, giving a cubic in Omega_Lambda (DIV ch26). SCH Fig. 13.4 shows the recollapse boundary. Observational confidence regions overlaid on the plane belong to physical-cosmology.

concepts.title: Fate of the universe
concepts.summary: Whether a Friedmann universe expands forever or recollapses follows from its curvature and contents: with Lambda = 0, closed models recollapse to a big crunch while flat and open ones expand forever; a positive Lambda eventually dominates any ever-expanding model and can make even a closed universe expand forever.
concepts.notes: DIV calls the expand-halt-recollapse models oscillating; all Lambda < 0 models are of this type, and a cyclic sequence of such arches is sometimes contemplated. All conclusions assume the cosmological principle holds on the largest scales.

concepts.title: Milne universe
concepts.summary: The empty Robertson-Walker model: with no matter and Lambda = 0, the Friedmann equation allows k = 0 with constant a (Minkowski space in ordinary coordinates) or k = -1 with a = t, which is again flat Minkowski spacetime sliced by hyperboloids of constant proper time from an origin.
concepts.notes: GA calls the k = 0 empty model Universe 0 and asks in Exercise 18.1 to show the Milne model is Minkowski space. Useful as a lesson that expansion can be a coordinate choice.

concepts.title: Friedmann equation for dust
aliases: master equation for dust and Lambda
concepts.summary: For pressureless matter plus a cosmological constant, conservation makes rho a^3 constant and the Friedmann equation becomes adot^2 = C/a + Lambda a^2/3 - k with C = (8 pi G/3) rho a^3; this single nonlinear equation generates the whole catalogue of classical model universes.
concepts.notes: Its general solution is elliptic, so books solve special cases exactly and the rest qualitatively. C sets the characteristic scales Lambda_c = 4/(9C^2), R_c = 3C/2 and the closed-model maximum radius R = C.

concepts.title: Einstein-de Sitter universe
concepts.summary: The spatially flat, Lambda = 0 universe containing only dust: a grows as t^(2/3), H = 2/(3t), the deceleration parameter is 1/2, and its age is 2/(3H_0). It sits exactly at critical density and describes the early behaviour of every dust big-bang model, since the matter term dominates at small a.
concepts.notes: DIV ch25 stresses early-time universality: near a = 0 every dust big-bang model grows like t^(2/3) regardless of k and Lambda (t^(1/2) if radiation dominates).

concepts.title: Radiation-dominated universe
concepts.summary: A flat universe whose gravity is dominated by radiation (rho proportional to a^-4, p = rho/3) expands as a proportional to t^(1/2) with H = 1/(2t), faster at early times than matter-dominated growth because pressure adds to the gravitating density; it begins from a = 0 with infinite density.
concepts.notes: DIV writes the radiation Friedmann equation as Rdot^2 = D/R^2 + Lambda R^2/3 - k with D constant. SCH notes a black-body temperature falls as 1/R. The thermal history of the radiation era belongs to physical-cosmology.

concepts.title: Matter-dominated era
concepts.summary: The epoch after radiation domination and before vacuum domination when pressureless matter controls the expansion, so rho a^3 is constant and, with curvature and Lambda negligible, the universe follows the Einstein-de Sitter law a proportional to t^(2/3).
concepts.notes: It necessarily follows radiation domination because radiation dilutes faster. GA ch49 places it in the Lambda-CDM timeline, ending when Lambda took over roughly 5 Gyr ago.

concepts.title: De Sitter universe
concepts.summary: The flat Robertson-Walker model containing only a positive cosmological constant: the Friedmann equation gives constant H = sqrt(Lambda/3) and exponential expansion a proportional to exp(Ht), with no big bang and no preferred epoch, since a time shift is undone by rescaling space.
concepts.notes: The earliest expanding model (1917). GA computes the curvature of the flat exponential metric first and then finds the source it requires. The same metric reappears as the steady-state model and as inflationary expansion; the flat slicing covers only half of the full de Sitter hyperboloid.

concepts.title: Vacuum domination and late-time exponential expansion
concepts.summary: In any ever-expanding model with positive Lambda, the constant vacuum term eventually outgrows matter and radiation, so the expansion approaches de Sitter behaviour with a proportional to exp(sqrt(Lambda/3) t); de Sitter is the late-time attractor of these models.
concepts.notes: For Lambda-CDM the asymptotic rate is H_0 sqrt(Omega_Lambda).

concepts.title: Flat matter-plus-Lambda universe
aliases: flat dust plus cosmological constant universe
concepts.summary: The k = 0 model with dust and a positive cosmological constant has the exact solution a proportional to [cosh(sqrt(3 Lambda) t) - 1]^(1/3) (equivalently sinh^(2/3)): it decelerates like Einstein-de Sitter at early times, passes through an inflection where attraction and repulsion balance, and then accelerates into de Sitter expansion.

names: flat dust plus cosmological constant universe

merged_from: flat dust plus cosmological constant universe
concepts.notes: The inflection (DIV "kink") also appears in open and closed models with positive Lambda. With observed parameters this is the late-time Lambda-CDM solution (DIV ch26); the model as the concordance cosmology belongs to physical-cosmology.

concepts.title: Negative cosmological constant universe
aliases: flat dust model with negative Lambda
concepts.summary: A flat dust model with Lambda < 0: the right-hand side of adot^2 = C/a + Lambda a^2/3 vanishes at a finite size, so the expansion halts and the universe recollapses, with a proportional to [1 - cos(sqrt(-3 Lambda) t)]^(1/3); a negative vacuum energy attracts like ordinary matter.

concepts.title: Closed Friedmann universe
concepts.summary: The k = +1, Lambda = 0 dust model whose spatial slices are 3-spheres: it expands from a big bang to a maximum radius set by its matter content and recollapses to a big crunch, with a cycloid solution a = (C/2)(1 - cos eta), t = (C/2)(eta - sin eta) in conformal time.

names: cycloid parametrization of the closed dust universe

merged_from: cycloid parametrization of the closed dust universe
concepts.notes: GA and DIV solve it with the substitution u^2 = a/C (implicit t(a) with arcsin); GA Exercise 19.8 (credited to Coleman) gives the conformal-time cycloid, which also shows a light ray has time to cross the universe once.

concepts.title: Open Friedmann universe
concepts.summary: The k = -1, Lambda = 0 dust model with hyperbolic spatial slices: it expands forever, starting like Einstein-de Sitter as t^(2/3) and approaching the coasting law a proportional to t at late times, when the curvature term dominates.
concepts.notes: The exact solution uses hyperbolic functions (arsinh), parallel to the closed case. Its late-time limit is the Milne universe.

concepts.title: Einstein static universe
concepts.summary: Einstein's 1917 static, spatially closed (R x S^3) universe in which a positive cosmological constant exactly balances the attraction of dust: staticity requires k = +1, Lambda = 1/a^2 and 4 pi G rho = Lambda, i.e. rho + 3p = 0 for the total content. Its metric, drawn as a cylinder, is also the standard backdrop for conformal diagrams.
concepts.notes: The model that motivated the Lambda term (partly on Machian grounds) and was abandoned after the discovery of expansion. DIV ch18 and GA ch19 reuse its metric as the arena into which Minkowski, de Sitter and Robertson-Walker spacetimes are conformally embedded.

concepts.title: Instability of the Einstein static universe
concepts.summary: Perturbing the scale factor about the Einstein static radius gives d^2(delta a)/dt^2 = Lambda delta a, so small disturbances grow exponentially: the static universe sits at a maximum of the effective potential and any slight excess or deficit of matter makes it collapse or expand.

names: instability of the Einstein static universe

merged_from: instability of the Einstein static universe
concepts.notes: Credited to Eddington (1930). GA Example 18.4 perturbs the acceleration equation with dust conservation; SCH Exercise 13.20 uses the effective potential.

concepts.title: Critical cosmological constant
concepts.summary: For closed dust models with Friedmann constant C, the value Lambda_c = 4/(9C^2) (the Einstein static value Lambda_E) at which the static solution exists at radius 3C/2; it divides closed models with positive Lambda into those that recollapse or bounce (below) and those that expand forever (above).
concepts.notes: GA and DIV use it as the reference value that labels the Lemaitre (above), Eddington-Lemaitre (equal) and bouncing (below) models.

concepts.title: Lemaitre universe
concepts.summary: A closed dust model with Lambda slightly above the critical value: it emerges from a big bang, loiters for a long time near the Einstein static radius where the expansion rate nearly vanishes, and then accelerates into de Sitter-like expansion; the closer Lambda is to critical, the longer the pause (growing like the logarithm of 1/epsilon).
concepts.notes: Historically Lemaitre's 1931 "primeval atom" model; it was one proposed fix of the time-scale problem because the loitering phase lengthens the age.

concepts.title: Eddington-Lemaitre universe
concepts.summary: The closed dust model with Lambda exactly critical: in one branch it starts arbitrarily close to the Einstein static state in the infinite past and then expands into exponential growth, so it has no big bang; the other branch starts from a big bang and approaches the static state asymptotically.
concepts.notes: Proposed by Eddington as a singularity-free alternative to Lemaitre's model.

concepts.title: Bouncing universe
concepts.summary: A closed dust model with 0 < Lambda < Lambda_c that contracts from very large size, reaches a nonzero minimum radius and re-expands exponentially without ever reaching a = 0; for the same parameters a separate branch expands from a big bang and recollapses, the two branches being separated by a forbidden region of the effective potential.
concepts.notes: Classical Lambda-driven bounce; quantum-gravity bounces belong to quantum-gravity-and-beyond.

concepts.title: De Sitter spacetime
aliases: hyperboloid embedding of de Sitter space
global coordinates of de Sitter space
flat slicing of de Sitter space
concepts.summary: The maximally symmetric vacuum solution with positive cosmological constant, realized globally as a one-sheeted hyperboloid in five-dimensional Minkowski space; in global coordinates its 3-sphere slices contract to a minimum radius sqrt(3/Lambda) and re-expand, while flat and static coordinates each cover only part of it.

names: de Sitter spacetime in static coordinates
hyperboloid embedding of de Sitter space
global coordinates of de Sitter space
flat slicing of de Sitter space
static coordinates of de Sitter space

merged_from: hyperboloid embedding of de Sitter space
global coordinates of de Sitter space
flat slicing of de Sitter space
static coordinates of de Sitter space
de Sitter spacetime in static coordinates
concepts.notes: The embedding makes the symmetry group visible as Lorentz transformations of the 5D space. Static coordinates give g_tt = 1 - H^2 r^2 with a horizon at r = 1/H, showing that the expansion of the flat form is a slicing effect (DIV ch25, GA Exercises 18.8 and 21.8). Flat (steady-state) coordinates cover only half the hyperboloid, bounded by a null surface. DIV ch13 notes it gives inertia with no matter, undercutting the Machian motivation for Lambda.

concepts.title: Penrose diagram of de Sitter space
aliases: square conformal diagram of de Sitter
concepts.summary: Conformally compactified, global de Sitter space maps onto a square strip of the Einstein static cylinder, with spacelike past and future null infinity as top and bottom edges; the flat (steady-state) slicing occupies half of this square.

names: Penrose diagram of de Sitter space

merged_from: Penrose diagram of de Sitter space
concepts.notes: Spacelike infinity explains why de Sitter observers have event horizons (GA ch19 Fig. 19.13, DIV ch25).

concepts.title: Anti-de Sitter spacetime
aliases: universal covering of anti-de Sitter space
concepts.summary: The maximally symmetric vacuum solution with negative cosmological constant: a hyperboloid in a flat five-dimensional space with two time directions, of constant negative curvature. Its periodic embedding time is unrolled to remove closed timelike curves, and its conformal boundary is timelike, so light reaches infinity and returns in finite time.

names: universal covering of anti-de Sitter space

merged_from: universal covering of anti-de Sitter space
concepts.notes: Global coordinates give -(1 + r^2) dt^2 + dr^2/(1 + r^2) + ... ; Poincare coordinates cover a patch with each constant-w slice conformal to Minkowski space. The universal cover changes topology from S^1 x R^3 to R^4 without changing local geometry. AdS as a holographic arena (AdS/CFT, boundary physics) belongs to quantum-gravity-and-beyond.

concepts.title: Big bang singularity
concepts.summary: In Friedmann models with rho + 3p > 0 (more generally rho + 3p > Lambda/(4 pi G)) that are expanding today, the acceleration equation makes a(t) concave, so the scale factor reached zero a finite time ago; there density and curvature diverge and the spacetime cannot be continued, which is conventionally chosen as t = 0.
concepts.notes: DIV ch24 proves the FRW result graphically: the present tangent to a concave a(t) hits zero a Hubble time ago, so a hits zero sooner. SCH argues via the effective potential and the radiation solution. Whether the singularity survives without exact symmetry (the general singularity theorems) belongs to causal-structure-and-singularities; the hot big bang as a physical history belongs to physical-cosmology.

concepts.title: Big crunch
concepts.summary: The final singularity of a recollapsing Friedmann universe, where the scale factor returns to zero after reaching a maximum: the time reverse of a big bang, drawn as a spacelike future boundary on the Penrose diagram.
concepts.notes: Occurs in closed Lambda <= 0 dust models, all Lambda < 0 models, and one branch of the bouncing family.

concepts.title: Hubble time
aliases: Hubble time as an age bound
concepts.summary: The reciprocal of the Hubble constant, t_H = 1/H_0 (about 14 billion years), the natural time scale of the expansion; if the expansion has always decelerated, the tangent to a(t) today reaches a = 0 one Hubble time ago, so the true age is shorter than 1/H_0.

names: Hubble time as an age bound

merged_from: Hubble time as an age bound

concepts.title: Age of the universe
aliases: cosmic time as a function of redshift
concepts.summary: The cosmic time elapsed since a = 0, found by separating variables in the dimensionless Friedmann equation: H_0 t_0 is an integral fixed by the density parameters, equal to 2/3 for Einstein-de Sitter and about 0.96 for a flat model with Omega_m = 0.3 and Omega_Lambda = 0.7. The same integral stopped at redshift z gives the cosmic time at which light was emitted.

names: cosmic time as a function of redshift

merged_from: cosmic time as a function of redshift
concepts.notes: DIV ch26 argues a cosmological constant relieves the tension with old-star ages because acceleration lengthens the age for given H_0.

concepts.title: Time-scale problem
concepts.summary: Before the 1950s the Hubble-time upper bound on the age of a decelerating universe (under 2 billion years with the then-accepted H_0) was shorter than the radiometric age of the Earth; proposed remedies included loitering Lemaitre or Eddington-Lemaitre models, and it was resolved by revised measurements of the Hubble constant.

concepts.title: Steady-state theory
aliases: exact Hubble law in the steady-state model
concepts.summary: The 1948 Bondi-Gold-Hoyle cosmology based on the perfect cosmological principle: the universe looks the same at all epochs, expanding with the exponential de Sitter metric while matter is continuously created to keep the density constant. It made sharp predictions, such as an exact linear Hubble law, and was ruled out chiefly by the cosmic microwave background.

names: exact Hubble law in the steady-state model

merged_from: exact Hubble law in the steady-state model
concepts.notes: In the steady-state metric luminosity distance equals z times the Hubble time exactly (DIV ch25). Its spacetime is only half of de Sitter and is past geodesically incomplete (causal-structure-and-singularities). Hoyle coined "Big Bang" on BBC radio in 1949 (GA margin note).

concepts.title: Hubble friction
concepts.summary: In an expanding universe the equation of a homogeneous scalar field, phiddot + 3H phidot + dU/dphi = 0, contains a term 3H phidot that acts like velocity-proportional friction on a ball rolling in the potential, reflecting the dilution of the field's kinetic energy by expansion; when H is large it keeps the field rolling slowly.
concepts.notes: Inflation, the inflaton and slow-roll belong to physical-cosmology; this concept is the dynamical effect itself.

concepts.title: Bianchi cosmologies
concepts.summary: Cosmological models that are spatially homogeneous but not isotropic: their slices are homogeneous under a three-dimensional symmetry group, classified into Bianchi types I to IX, and the field equations reduce to ordinary differential equations in time.

concepts.title: Kasner metric
concepts.summary: The vacuum Bianchi type I solution ds^2 = dt^2 - t^(2p1) dx^2 - t^(2p2) dy^2 - t^(2p3) dz^2 with p1 + p2 + p3 = p1^2 + p2^2 + p3^2 = 1, which expands in some directions while contracting in another and has cigar or pancake singularities.
concepts.notes: Oscillatory Kasner epochs near generic singularities (BKL) belong to causal-structure-and-singularities.
